title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A call opens with namaste — the word M2 taught for arriving and leaving both, and the word a spoken-Sanskrit speaker genuinely says when the phone is picked up. There is no separate telephone greeting in this language, and this course will not invent one.

dūrabhāṣaḥ is a MODERN word, and you should know that while you learn it. It was coined in the twentieth century by the spoken-Sanskrit movement out of dūra ('far') and bhāṣa ('speech'), because there were no telephones in the language's classical life. It is the word people use; it is not an ancient one.
A caller names himself in the plain naming shape: aham rāmaḥ vadāmi, 'I, Rāma, am speaking'. There is no separate word for 'this is' and no special form for a name on the phone.

kaḥ asks 'who' of a man and kā of a woman — the question word itself changes, which no question word in L1 did. M2's kim covered every question that level asked; a call is the first job that genuinely needs to ask who.
vadati is 'speaks': vadāmi when it is me, vadatu when it is a request. One verb, the same three endings the course has been building on since M4, and it is what a call is made of.
śṛṇoti is 'hears' and śṛṇomi is 'I hear'. A bad line is aham na śṛṇomi, with na in front of the verb exactly where M2 put it.

The telephone you speak BY takes the by-ending M4 opened: dūrabhāṣeṇa vadati is 'speaks on the telephone'. It is the same -ena that sits on yānena and jalena, and the telephone is a means of speaking in exactly the way a vehicle is a means of travelling.

saṃdeśaḥ is a message, and it is a modern use of an old word in the same way dūrabhāṣaḥ is a modern word. Its nasal is written INSIDE the token, which is correct: that is a join inside one word, like the one in saṃskṛtam. The rule this course holds is only that no word ENDS in it.
The call closes with the two words M1 and M2 already gave: dhanyavādaḥ and namaste. The same greeting that opened it closes it, which is the cheapest thing in this course and the most used.

Both sides of the call speak the polite register, all the way through: bhavān or bhavatī with a third-person verb. English drops into first names on the phone almost at once; here the address does not move, and a name is never used to call somebody's attention because this course opens no vocative at all.

words.note: 'Speaks'. Here as vadāmi, 'I speak', which is what a caller says about himself. vadatu is the request shape, and all three are one word and one row.
M2's greeting, opening a phone call. There is no telephone word in this language, and a spoken-Sanskrit speaker really does answer with this one.
M1's name in its plain naming shape, sitting beside aham with nothing joining them. English needs 'this is'; here the two words simply stand together.

sentences.trap: English answers a phone with a word that means nothing else — 'hello' is for telephones and doorways and little else. namaste is the ordinary greeting doing an extra job, so nothing here is special to a phone at all.
sentences.sound: na-mas-TE. a-HAM RAA-mah va-DAA-mi. vadāmi has a short first a and a long second one: va-DAA-mi.

variations.changed: a woman names herself, and only the name changes — vadāmi never agreed with gender
the greeting drops, which is what happens when the call has already been answered
M2's other greeting opens instead — a shade more formal and equally ordinary

mistake.why: The name has been cut back to its bare stem. A caller names himself in the naming shape, rāmaḥ — the shape that ends -aḥ is not decoration, it is what makes the word the subject of the sentence.

sentences.usage: The first thing said on either end of a call, by the person who dialled and by the person who picked up.
sentences.mnemonic: vadāmi is what you DO on a phone, and it ends in the same -mi as gacchāmi and paṭhāmi. Nothing about the telephone changes the verb.

words.note: 'Who', and it forks: kaḥ asks about a man, kā about a woman. M2's kim asked everything L1 needed; a phone call is the first place that has to ask who.
M2's polite 'you'. There is no verb in this question at all — two words in the naming shape, side by side, are a complete sentence in this language.
Not in this sentence, and that is the point. kim asks what; kaḥ asks who, and the two have never been the same question.

sentences.trap: There is no verb here and there does not need to be. English cannot ask 'who is this?' without 'is'; this language sets the question word beside the person and stops.
sentences.sound: KAH bha-VAAN. Both words end in the light breath this course writes -aḥ and -n; neither is stressed hard.

variations.changed: the person asked is a woman, so BOTH words fork — the question word as well as the address
a verb is added and the address drops, which is the blunter version of the same question

variations.cue: Who is speaking on the telephone?
variations.changed: the means is named, using the by-ending M4 opened

mistake.why: kaḥ is the shape used of a man. Asked of a woman it is kā bhavatī — the question word agrees with who is being asked, which is a thing no L1 question word did.

sentences.usage: Asked when the voice is not recognised, and not thought rude.

words.note: Here as kā, asked of a woman. The two shapes are one word and one row, exactly as bhavān and bhavatī were in M2.
M1's name, answering in the same naming shape rāmaḥ used. A name does not change because it is spoken into a telephone.
vadāmi again, unchanged for a woman speaking. The verb in this language marks person and never gender in the present.

sentences.trap: Two things forked in the first half and nothing forked in the second. kā and bhavatī both moved because a woman is being asked; vadāmi did not move at all, because a present-tense verb here never notices gender.

variations.changed: the whole exchange between two men, with both halves of the fork going the other way

variations.cue: Who is this? The teacher speaking.
variations.changed: the answer is a role rather than a name, in the same naming shape
the verb drops and two naming words answer on their own, exactly as the question was asked

sentences.usage: The whole of a phone opening, in two turns, with the register never moving off bhavatī.

words.note: 'Hears'. śṛṇomi is 'I hear'. Between them they are most of what gets said on a bad line, and neither needs an object to be a complete sentence.
The polite 'you' with its third-person verb, which is the register this course has spoken since M2 and does not leave on the telephone.
M2's yes/no marker at the front. It is what makes this a question rather than a report that somebody can hear.

sentences.trap: There is no 'me' in this sentence. English needs an object — 'can you hear ME' — and here the verb stands alone, because what is being asked is whether hearing is happening at all.
sentences.sound: KIM bha-VAAN SHRI-no-ti. The śṛ- of śṛṇoti is a sh followed by the short ri vowel, all in one beat.

variations.changed: asked of a woman; the address forks and the verb does not
kim drops and the question becomes the relieved statement that follows it

variations.cue: Can you hear me? Yes, I can hear you.
variations.changed: the answer is added, and the ending swings from -ti to -mi because the person hearing is now the one speaking

mistake.why: -mi is 'I'. This asks whether I hear your honour, which is the opposite question. The ending has to follow whoever is doing the hearing.

sentences.usage: The first thing said when the line is bad, and often the only thing said for a while.

sentences.display: aham na śṛṇomi. kṛpayā punaḥ vadatu.
sentences.script: अहम् न शृणोमि। कृपया पुनः वदतु।
sentences.cue: I can't hear you. Please say that again.
sentences.literal: I not hear. please again let-speak

words.note: Here as śṛṇomi with na in front of it. Negation in this course has been one word in front of the verb since M2, and it has not changed.
Here as vadatu, the request shape. Asking somebody to repeat themselves is an ordinary request and carries the ordinary -tu.
M5's 'again', which did the work of 'more' at a table and does the work of 'repeat' on a telephone. The word did not change; the verb in front of it did.

sentences.trap: 'Say that again' has no 'that' in it. punaḥ vadatu is 'speak again', and the thing to be repeated is never named — which is how this course also said 'more food'.
sentences.sound: a-HAM NA SHRI-no-mi. kri-PA-yaa PU-nah va-DA-tu. The second half is said faster, the way a request usually is.

variations.changed: the complaint stands alone and the request is left to be understood
the request stands alone, which is the politer half to say first

variations.display: sā na śṛṇoti. kṛpayā punaḥ vadatu.
variations.script: सा न शृणोति। कृपया पुनः वदतु।
variations.cue: She can't hear you. Please say that again.
variations.changed: somebody else is the one who cannot hear, so the ending moves to -ti and the request does not move at all

sentences.usage: Said without apology. Asking for a repetition is not an admission of anything in this register.

words.note: 'Telephone', built from dūra ('far') and bhāṣa ('speech'). It is a twentieth-century coinage, not a classical word. Here in the by-shape: you speak BY the telephone.
The plain third-person shape, reporting about somebody who is not the speaker. This is the sentence you say to the person standing next to you, not into the phone.
M1's name as the subject. A compound noun in the by-shape sits between the subject and the verb with nothing marking it as an instrument except its own ending.

sentences.trap: English needs a preposition — ON the telephone — and here the whole of it is the -ena at the end of the word. Looking for a separate word to carry 'on' is looking for something that is not there.
sentences.sound: SEE-taa doo-ra-BHAA-she-na VA-da-ti. dūrabhāṣeṇa is six beats; the ṣ is a sh made with the tongue curled back.

variations.changed: the person speaking changes, and the instrument's ending does not notice
the speaker reports on themselves, so -ti becomes -mi
the telephone stops being the means and becomes the thing talked about, so it goes back to its naming shape

mistake.why: The telephone is left in its naming shape, which makes it a second subject. The means of doing something takes the -ena M4 opened — the same ending as yānena and jalena.

sentences.usage: Said about somebody, not to them: this is the line you get when you ask for a person who is already on another call.

words.note: Here in the naming shape, as the thing being described rather than the thing spoken by. Its -aḥ is what the adjective has to match.
M3's 'new', agreeing with a masculine word and so ending -aḥ. A modern word takes the ordinary adjective paradigm like any other.
Here as mama, 'my'. mama X asti is how this course has said 'I have X' since M3, and it says it about a telephone the same way.

variations.changed: M3's purāṇaḥ replaces navaḥ, and it agrees the same way

variations.cue: I do not have a telephone.
variations.changed: the adjective drops and na denies the whole thing, which is this course's way of saying you do not have something
M2's 'of your honour' takes the place of mama, and the rest of the sentence is untouched

sentences.usage: Small talk, and the one sentence in the module that is not part of a call.

sentences.cue: There is a message for you.

words.note: 'A message' — an old word doing a modern job. Its nasal is written inside the token, which is a join inside one word and correct; no word in this course ENDS in one.
M5's 'to your honour', the shape that carried the liking frame and carries this one. bhavatyai is the same thing said to a woman.
M3's 'there is'. The message exists and somebody is the one it exists FOR, which is the whole of the construction.

sentences.trap: This is a 'there is' sentence with a person attached, not a 'you have' sentence. The message is the subject; your honour is only who it is for — the same shape of thought as the liking frame from M1.

variations.cue: There is a message for you.
variations.changed: said to a woman, so bhavate becomes bhavatyai — and the message does not move
the 'to' shape gives way to the 'my' shape, and the sentence becomes possession rather than delivery

variations.cue: There is no message for you.
variations.changed: na in front of asti denies the whole thing, exactly as M3 taught

sentences.usage: Said by whoever answered the phone earlier, to the person it was for.

sentences.display: rāmaḥ gṛhe na asti. kṛpayā punaḥ dūrabhāṣeṇa vadatu.
sentences.script: रामः गृहे न अस्ति। कृपया पुनः दूरभाषेण वदतु।
sentences.cue: Rāma is not at home. Please call again.
sentences.literal: Rāma at-home not is. please again by-telephone let-speak

words.note: In the by-shape again, now inside a request. 'Call again' in this course is 'speak again by telephone' — there is no separate verb for telephoning.
Here as gṛhe, 'at home'. M6 gave three shapes of this word and this is the one for where somebody is, as against gṛham for where they are going.
'Again' doing its third job in three modules: more food, say it again, call again. One small word covering what English spreads over three.

sentences.trap: 'Call again' is built out of nothing new: punaḥ from M5, dūrabhāṣeṇa from four sentences ago, and the -tu ending from M1. A learner looking for a verb meaning 'to telephone' is looking for a word this language did not need.
sentences.sound: RAA-mah GRI-he NA AS-ti. kri-PA-yaa PU-nah doo-ra-BHAA-she-na va-DA-tu. The first half is said flat, the second with the small lift a request carries.

variations.display: sītā gṛhe na asti. kṛpayā punaḥ dūrabhāṣeṇa vadatu.
variations.script: सीता गृहे न अस्ति। कृपया पुनः दूरभाषेण वदतु।
variations.cue: Sītā is not at home. Please call again.
variations.changed: the person who is out changes, and nothing else in either half moves
na drops and the call succeeds, which is the other half of this exchange

variations.display: rāmaḥ gṛhe na asti. kṛpayā sāyam punaḥ vadatu.
variations.script: रामः गृहे न अस्ति। कृपया सायम् पुनः वदतु।
variations.cue: Rāma is not at home. Please call again in the evening.
variations.changed: a time is added out of M4's stock, and the telephone is left unsaid because it is obvious

mistake.display: rāmaḥ gṛham na asti. kṛpayā punaḥ dūrabhāṣeṇa vadatu.
mistake.why: gṛham is where you are GOING; gṛhe is where you ARE. M6 opened both shapes and this sentence needs the second one — being at home is not motion towards it.

sentences.usage: The answer given to a caller by whoever is in the house, and the politest form of it.

words.note: The same word that opened the call, closing it. This is the cheapest thing M2 taught and it has now paid for itself in every module of the course.
L2-M1's thanks. On a telephone it does the work of English 'all right then' as much as of 'thank you' — it marks that the business of the call is over.
M6's word of agreement, one module old and already the natural way to close. It accepts whatever was just said without repeating any of it.

sentences.trap: Three separate words, each a complete utterance, said one after another. English strings a closing together — 'all right then, thanks, bye' — and this language puts full stops between them.
sentences.sound: AS-tu. dhan-ya-VAA-dah. na-mas-TE. Each is said on its own, with a real pause between, and the last one falls away.

variations.changed: astu drops, which is what happens when there was nothing to agree to
the thanks drops and the close is two words, which is the commonest length
the close carries an instruction instead of a farewell, using M6's plan words

sentences.usage: How a call ends, and the last words either side says.
sentences.mnemonic: namaste opens the call and namaste closes it. One word, two doors.

comprehensionPool.cue: Hello. This is the teacher speaking.
Who is speaking on the telephone?

comprehensionPool.display: sā na śṛṇoti. kṛpayā punaḥ vadatu.
comprehensionPool.script: सा न शृणोति। कृपया पुनः वदतु।
comprehensionPool.cue: She cannot hear. Please say that again.
My brother is on the telephone.

comprehensionPool.display: bhavate saṃdeśaḥ asti. kṛpayā punaḥ dūrabhāṣeṇa vadatu.
comprehensionPool.script: भवते संदेशः अस्ति। कृपया पुनः दूरभाषेण वदतु।
comprehensionPool.cue: There is a message for you. Please call again.

comprehensionPool.display: rāmaḥ dūrabhāṣeṇa vadati, kintu aham na śṛṇomi.
comprehensionPool.script: रामः दूरभाषेण वदति, किन्तु अहम् न शृणोमि।
comprehensionPool.cue: Rāma is speaking on the telephone, but I cannot hear him.
The teacher is on the telephone.
Please call again in the evening.

comprehensionPool.display: sītā gṛhe na asti. saṃdeśaḥ asti.
comprehensionPool.script: सीता गृहे न अस्ति। संदेशः अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: Sītā is not at home. There is a message.
Is there a message? Yes, there is.
